indexDescription: Check a KakoBuy find against its original listing, selected option and warehouse photographs.
faq: What does a KakoBuy QC finder match?

A finder can use the underlying marketplace listing to locate photographs linked to earlier orders. First match the marketplace and item ID. Then check whether the pictures identify the same size, colour and version as the one you are considering.
Is the number in this catalogue page address the Weidian item ID?
The number in a Sheet Grid page address identifies that catalogue page. Open the original seller link and read the itemID value there before using a Weidian QC lookup.
What should I do if an agent link contains an encoded seller URL?

Open the product normally and use its original marketplace link when available. Compare the destination, shop and item number with the saved row. Avoid guessing which digits in a long agent URL identify the product.
Can an image match find the exact seller?

An image match can suggest visually similar rows. Several shops can use the same photograph. Compare seller identity and marketplace item ID before assigning any historical warehouse photographs to the result.
Do older QC photos show the item I will receive?

Earlier photos can reveal what someone received from a listing at that time. Only evidence tied to your own order can show the unit assigned to you. Record the age, option and visible limitations of a reference.
What does a blank QC result mean?

It means that search produced no usable reference for your query. Check the marketplace, item number and link type. An empty search does not tell you whether an inspection exists in a private order or whether a product is in stock.
Can a copied item link preserve my selected size?
Reopen the link and inspect the selectors. If it opens with a default size, save the original option text and your intended size separately. Verify them again in the order summary.
How can I tell whether a row describes a set or a single piece?

Read the selected option beside its live price. Identify the pieces listed for that option and compare them with the summary. A photograph of a model in a matching outfit can represent items sold separately.
Why do two listings show exactly the same studio photograph?
Sellers can use common imagery. Compare their shop names, IDs, option names and size charts separately. Keep a screenshot under the listing it came from even when another page shows the same garment.
Which clothing label should I ask to see?
Specify the purpose. A neckline size label shows the marked size; a care label may provide composition or care instructions. Ask for a full view in context and a close-up with legible text.
Does a size tag confirm fit?
Compare the actual garment measurements with a piece that fits. Use the seller's measurement diagram and consistent endpoints. The same marked size can correspond to different patterns.
How should a tape be positioned for an underarm-width photo?
Request the garment laid flat and relaxed, with the tape crossing between the corresponding underarm seam points. Both ends and the units should be visible in one frame.
How can I compare two shoes in a single pair?

Ask for both shoes together, aligned at their heels and photographed from above. Use additional views to check each label and the feature of concern. A single shoe cannot establish that its partner matches.
What makes a shoe-label photo readable?
Ask for one label per shoe with the printed size and sizing system in focus. Save each picture under its left or right identifier. Watch for EU, US and UK sizes sharing one label.
What should I do if an advertised accessory appears to be missing?
Save the exact option description showing that it includes the accessory. Ask for an overview of the full contents and a check of pockets or inner packaging before reporting a shortage.
Which details belong in a custom photo request?

Give the order reference, selected option, view required and the decision it will resolve. For measurements, add endpoints and units. Check service availability and the displayed price before confirming.
Can a warehouse photo confirm the true colour on my screen?
Lighting, white balance and screen settings influence appearance. Compare several views and the seller's colour label. If two options only differ by shade, ask for a view with the identifier visible.
How should I record a replacement order?
Keep the original case reference and give the replacement a separate entry. Record the replacement's option, intake reference and pictures. Recheck the original problem on the new unit.
What if the seller edits an option after I pay?
Keep the dated selection screenshot and order confirmation from payment. Compare the received item against that record, then show the changed listing separately when asking for a check.
Should I discard the retail packaging before deciding about an exchange?
Ask the applicable service or seller which tags, bags and boxes must accompany the item. Keep those materials until you understand the conditions for the specific order.
Where should I take a question about an actual KakoBuy order?

Use the support channel in your KakoBuy account with the purchase or parcel reference. This independent catalogue can help identify a listing, while the account record contains the transaction details.

articles.title: KakoBuy QC lookup: matching a photograph by marketplace and item ID
articles.lead: A number can narrow a search from thousands of similar product photographs to one seller listing. It is most useful when you also retain the marketplace, the selected option and the date of the reference.
sections: Identify the number you actually have

Start on the purchase page for the product you mean to investigate. Follow the original seller link and record its marketplace. A Weidian listing can carry an itemID value in the seller URL. The smaller number at the end of a Sheet Grid catalogue page identifies a different record. An agent order reference, domestic tracking number and warehouse intake reference also serve different purposes. Keep their names beside them when copying numbers to your notes.
Run a lookup with the source attached

Use the complete source product link where a QC finder accepts it. If a service asks for a marketplace and number separately, use the pair from the same original listing. Save both the search input and the result so another person can reproduce your comparison. A result reached only by typing a broad garment name is a candidate for review. Compare its original seller identifier before attaching the photos to your intended order.
Test what the album can establish

Suppose the listing has a black jacket and a navy version with a different lining. An old front photograph might confirm the shape of the pockets. Without the option label or a visible lining it cannot settle which version was photographed. Describe the strongest observation you can make, such as two flap pockets visible. Keep a separate note for the unresolved question, such as the material on the inside of the navy version.
Handle empty and conflicting results

Check the marketplace, the intact item number and whether you copied an item link rather than a shop homepage or an image URL. A finder may have no public album for an otherwise valid listing. If two albums conflict, compare dates, options, packaging and the particular detail visible. A seller can update a listing over time, or a gallery may mix options. Do not average inconsistent evidence into a confident claim.
Move from reference to order evidence

Before purchase, decide whether the missing detail matters enough to ask the seller or leave the item on your shortlist. After purchase, use the photographs tied to your own order for decisions about the received unit. Retain the older album as a comparison and clearly label its origin. If the new unit differs, identify the specific feature and quote your selected option, rather than promising support that the historical picture describes every item now supplied.
Make the search repeatable

Imagine a friend sends a cropped photo of a brown overshirt. The corner shows part of an item number. Searching that partial number might produce a page with an overshirt, but several digits or even the marketplace could be missing. Ask for the product link that accompanied the photo. If your friend only has the image, create a visual-reference note and leave its seller blank. The distinction matters weeks later when you are deciding whether to buy a listing that happens to resemble the picture.

A repeatable lookup has a simple test. A second person, given only the public listing reference, should be able to follow the same route to the same offer or report that the offer has since changed. Record the date, marketplace name, complete identifier and public gallery address where available. A friend should never need your account password or access to your payment history to reproduce a public product search. Keep purchase-specific checks in your private order record instead.
Check the gallery against a feature you can distinguish

Choose a detail before opening a gallery. For the overshirt, the relevant question might be whether a button sits on each cuff or whether the cuff closes with a snap. Look for an angle where the closure is open and the inside surface is visible. A front photograph with the sleeves folded underneath may show the cloth colour and approximate cut while telling you nothing about either cuff. Describe what is visible separately from what you infer from the seller description.

Consider how two photos could disagree without either being altered. A photograph of the brown option may show dark fasteners and one of the cream option may show pale fasteners. The gallery could then contain two visually different cuffs under one marketplace item ID. Check the option tag if one exists. Where it is missing, use the photos to formulate a more precise question for the seller, such as whether the brown option currently has dark buttons at both cuffs.
Read dates in context

A photograph's publication date and the date a buyer received the item need not coincide. When a finder supplies only one date, write down the label beside the date. Avoid assigning the image to a particular production run unless the source actually supplies that information. If the seller page recently acquired a new colour name, an old gallery result is still a reference for the listing, but the connection to the new option needs separate evidence. Do not rename an older image to match the newer choice.

For a simple comparison, write two dated lines. One could say that the album seen on Monday showed a brown overshirt with two visible chest pockets. The other could say that on Thursday the seller offered a brown option whose description mentioned one chest pocket. The two lines preserve the disagreement precisely. A support question can now ask which pocket arrangement applies to the presently selected brown option without arguing about whether the entire listing is accurate.
Read the gaps in an otherwise convincing album

Several photographs can all originate from the same unit. Five angles of a garment spread on a green table give more information about that garment, but they do not establish that five buyers received it. Look for shared folds, identical tags and repeated packing labels when assessing the range of examples. Count distinct units only when the source gives you a basis for doing so. Otherwise describe the number of useful views and avoid implying that you assessed a larger sample.

A series can also omit precisely the feature that matters. A bag might be shown from the front, back and both sides while its interior remains closed. The gallery could resolve whether it has external side pockets and leave the number of interior compartments unanswered. Save the picture that best shows the external pockets. Write down the interior question beside it so the next stage of your research addresses that missing detail instead of repeating a search that has already yielded all it can.
Bring the correct comparison back to your order

Once your own warehouse record is available, start a separate folder or note for the received item. Include the selected option as it appeared on the order, then add your observations about the received unit. If the newly photographed garment has an unexpected cuff, compare its label and the specific closure against the saved seller option. The old public image can illustrate what prompted your initial question. Your paid selection and your own photographs explain the actual order difference.

For a message requesting clarification, supply only the pieces someone needs to act. Identify the order privately, name the selected option, describe the visible detail and ask for the missing view or confirmation. A message such as “Please show the open left cuff of the brown overshirt so I can see whether it closes with a button” gives the reader a clear action. If the current photo answers the question, close the note with that observation and its date.

articles.title: KakoBuy item ID versus size and colour: preserving the exact choice
articles.lead: A seller can place many combinations on one product page. The marketplace identifier finds that page; a saved selection explains which one of those combinations you wanted.
sections: Separate three records

Keep the seller listing, the selected option text and the paid order summary. The first record identifies an offer, the second identifies a choice within it, and the third shows what was submitted. An internal stock keeping unit may be visible for some selections. When no SKU is displayed, do not manufacture one by inventing a number or appending a colour name to the item link.
Change one selector at a time

Open the listing and choose a colour while holding size constant. Observe whether the image, available sizes, price or quantity changes. Now change size and repeat. Two almost identical labels can refer to different fabric, an earlier model or a version sold without accessories. Keep the original seller wording as well as any translation. The word black alone rarely distinguishes two black choices if the seller uses a suffix to separate them.
Reopen the copied link

Copy the source link and open it in a fresh tab. If the page starts at a default selection, the link is useful for finding the listing but does not preserve your choice. Keep the option notes beside it. If a link appears to restore a choice, still confirm the order summary before payment. A prior selection in a shopping session or an edited listing can affect what a returning visitor sees.
Compare options as complete combinations

Imagine one row showing trousers, a jacket and a complete suit. The cheapest price could correspond to the trousers. Add the exact jacket-and-trousers option before comparing its subtotal with a different shop's full suit. For quantities, record complete sets separately from pieces. Two units of a suit and two individual garments represent different orders even when a cart shows the number two in both cases.
Match the warehouse entry to the selection

When photographs arrive, identify the order and the option on the received unit. A size label can support a size check, while a picture showing both pieces helps confirm a set. Ask for the missing feature in a new view if the existing picture does not resolve the question. An item ID match is a necessary link in the evidence chain, but it cannot select a colour or count an accessory for you.
Read a listing as a collection of choices

Suppose you are comparing two canvas bags that share one marketplace link. The seller offers short and long handles in two colours, then a separate choice between a bag alone and a bag with a removable pouch. Choosing green does not settle the handle length or whether you are buying a pouch. Read through all visible selectors after making a colour choice. Some combinations may disappear or change names as a result of the preceding selection. Save the complete final wording in the order the seller displays it.

An internal SKU is helpful when the seller actually exposes one. It might identify a particular combination even when two translated option names look alike. Treat it as a literal identifier, including any leading zeroes or letters. A spreadsheet that interprets the value as a number can discard part of it. Store the value as text and reopen the file to confirm it survived. If the seller never displays an internal code, the marketplace link plus the precise option text and dated order confirmation can still be an adequate record.
Observe what the selected price buys

At the top of a multi-option listing, a displayed price may be a starting point. Select the exact components you want, then note the amount and quantity alongside that selection. In the canvas bag example, a photo might show the pouch clipped inside the bag while the cheapest choice sells the pouch alone. Copying the headline price beside a photo of the set would produce a misleading comparison. A row labelled “green bag, long handles, pouch included, one set” gives the price a defined unit.

Quantity deserves a separate check. If you want two people to receive one complete set each, first confirm how many bags and pouches one unit of the selected option contains. Place the desired quantity in the cart and inspect the resulting selection and subtotal before deciding. A free-text instruction about including a pouch does not establish that you paid for the option containing it. If the combination you want has disappeared, ask which listing currently offers it and start a new comparison for that listing.
Use translations without losing distinguishing details

Machine translation can make two option strings read identically even when the original includes an extra character, a model suffix or a different unit. Save both original labels and your working translations, with the original spelling intact. Note the option order only as a temporary aid. A seller can rearrange choices, so “third tile from the left” may describe the wrong product when you return. An image thumbnail can help locate a choice, but its colour or pictured accessories need confirmation from the selected option text.

If the language difference affects a practical decision, make the question concrete. For example, ask whether the two green long-handle options differ in pouch inclusion or in bag dimensions. Include their original option text so the respondent can distinguish them. A broad question asking which version is better may produce an opinion without resolving the specific difference. Keep the answer with its source and date. If it refers to one colour, avoid applying it to every colour on the listing.
Distinguish the selection from a customer's note

A configurable product sometimes invites a buyer to leave instructions. The instruction and the selected item perform different jobs. The selected option establishes what the cart and receipt describe; a note communicates something you have requested. If you select a short-handle bag and type “long handle please” in a message, the records may point in different directions. Before paying, choose the exact available option or seek a written explanation of how the seller handles the requested combination.

For a gift with several components, create a short record for each intended recipient. Record their chosen colour, handle length, pouch choice and quantity, even if the marketplace URL is identical for everyone. Confirm the final order has the expected number of distinct lines. Two identical green bags may legitimately appear on one line with quantity two. Green bags with different handle lengths need a way to distinguish those selections in the record you will use at warehouse intake.
Resolve mismatches at the right level

When a received item differs, ask first whether the listing, the selected combination or the received unit is in question. A correct item number with the wrong colour points to an option-level issue. A correct colour with a missing pouch raises a package-content question. An entirely different seller item number is a source-link discrepancy. Each needs different evidence, and naming the precise difference makes a follow-up easier for the person handling the order.

For the bag example, gather the paid order line showing the pouch-inclusive combination, the warehouse photo showing the bag, and any photograph that lets you inspect its interior. If the bag is closed, describe the pouch as unconfirmed and ask for an open view if available. If a clear view of the contents and an item count confirms the pouch is absent, update the note. Your record now connects the specific option purchased to the specific feature you needed to verify.

articles.title: How to recover the seller listing behind a KakoBuy link
articles.lead: An agent link is convenient for checkout. The original marketplace page gives you a separate reference for the seller, the listing identifier and the options you are researching.
sections: Work from the item page

Start with the specific product rather than the platform homepage, an affiliate registration page or a search results page. Open the product normally and look for an original listing link. On this grid, use the source-link control on the detail page when it is available. Copy the resulting address to a private note. If the destination is simply a shop, return to the item and identify the product inside that shop before doing a QC lookup.
Recognize an embedded URL

Some KakoBuy item links include an encoded marketplace address in a url parameter. Percent-encoded characters can make it look unfamiliar: an encoded question mark or equals sign still belongs to the embedded address. A finder may accept the complete agent link directly. Prefer an exposed original-link control when possible, and inspect the resulting destination rather than deleting punctuation until a URL happens to open.
Verify the recovered destination

Compare the seller domain, item number, title, pictures and available options. A convincing title alone is insufficient when several shops sell similarly named items. An agent URL and its seller URL need not look alike, but the marketplace identity and item number should reconcile where both expose them. Save the pair under one note and give the note a recognizable label such as blue jacket with two-way zip.
Distinguish useful metadata from private order information

A public listing reference is usually sufficient for comparing a find. Do not share an account dashboard URL, a checkout page containing personal information or a screenshot with an address to prove a simple listing match. Crop any evidence you share to the item and option. An exchange or payment inquiry belongs in the official order channel, where the corresponding order reference can be supplied privately.
Deal with an unavailable listing

A seller may remove a product or restrict what an anonymous visitor can see. Record the page state and date. If a visual search returns another shop, create a new entry instead of replacing the old source link under the same name. The new listing needs its own price, size, option and QC checks. An old warehouse album attached to the first seller cannot establish what the second seller will deliver.
Give each address a purpose

A public product find can generate several addresses that look plausible in isolation. The spreadsheet has its own page for the item, the agent can show a product detail page, and the original seller lists the product on a marketplace. A link to the product image opens a fourth destination. Use meaningful field names when you save them. “Spreadsheet discovery page,” “agent purchase page” and “original marketplace offer” are more useful a week later than three unlabeled links in a chat.

A common test is to imagine which page you would open to answer a question about the seller's current options. A standalone image can show the bag pictured in an advertisement. It cannot establish whether the merchant still offers a red version with a shoulder strap. A catalogue card can help you return to the find, but its short description may omit a seller option. Keep the sources that serve each purpose and record which one supplied a particular observation about the product.
Follow a normal redirect carefully

A shared link may go through a redirect before reaching a product. Open it as an ordinary public listing and note the final destination. Read the address bar alongside the actual content on the page. A shop landing page featuring a similar product in a carousel does not identify that carousel entry as the original item. Look for a specific product title, item identifier and selection controls. If you reach a sign-in page, keep the original public reference and note that the destination could not be confirmed from that session.

Avoid sending an entire browser or order export to someone who only needs to identify a product. If the item link lives inside a purchase history, use the public product or original link control and check its destination before sharing. A screenshot of the whole order history may include unrelated products, names or payment details. The marketplace label and public item reference normally give another person a much cleaner starting point for an independent check of the seller listing.
Recognize a link that opens at the wrong level

Imagine a short link opens a seller's collection of storage boxes. The image of a green box looks familiar, but selecting it reveals a page with several sizes and lids sold separately. You have found a candidate, not yet a recovered link. Compare its marketplace number with any identifier in the original product record. Check whether the seller name and available configurations align with what you saved. If the original record has no identifier, describe the new link as a possible match and explain the basis.

A seller can have more than one listing for nearly identical boxes. One might sell sample units, another bulk sets. A product photo can survive across both listings while prices, quantities and dimensions differ. Using the currently accessible offer as a substitute for the old one may be a reasonable buying decision after a fresh review. Replacing the saved original URL without noting the substitution, however, would assign older warehouse photographs and purchase details to a different commercial offer.
Check what survives when the link is shared

If the item opens with a selected size in your session, copy its public address into a fresh tab. See whether it preserves the selected option or returns to a default page. A session can remember choices that are absent from the URL. Ask a collaborator to choose the exact option text in their own session if they need to confirm a price or photograph. Do not assume their first displayed option matches yours merely because the marketplace page has the same item number.

For the storage box, keep the length, width, height and lid choice beside the link. If the seller uses a label such as “large with lid,” preserve that exact wording and add the dimensions separately. If the link later shows an amended size chart, the original observation remains traceable to a date. You can then decide whether the current offer still serves your purpose, without having to reconstruct why an earlier buyer associated a particular capacity or price with the shared address.
Leave a useful result when recovery fails

A useful record can end with an unresolved source. Write down the last confirmed public location and what stopped the search, such as a removed product page or a redirect to a shop. Keep any item identifier you can independently read from the original link. Distinguish a seller claim that the item moved from a verified replacement link that the seller supplied. If you later receive that replacement, open a separate record and connect the two with the date and explanation.

Before using a recovered link to make a purchase, review the current price, package quantity and selected option. A recovered historical URL answers the question of where the original find pointed. The product offered there today still merits its own review. For a purchase already in progress, use the order's private support channel and attach only the relevant original and current product evidence. A public QC search and an account-specific order question can then be resolved independently.

articles.title: Same photo, different listing: comparing two KakoBuy spreadsheet finds
articles.lead: Identical studio images can lead to different shops, sizes and packages. Compare what each seller actually offers before using a visual match as evidence about the goods.
sections: Start with the source pair

Save both seller links and identify their marketplace listing numbers. A repeat of the same listing across two catalogue pages is different from two separate sellers reusing a studio image. If the links point to one listing, investigate whether your notes refer to different options or snapshots taken at different dates. If the listings differ, keep two independent evidence records even if the thumbnail is identical down to the background.
Look past the most recognizable feature

A front graphic, colour or model pose works well for finding candidates. It is less useful for deciding whether the construction is the same. Compare objective features such as pocket shape, number of seams, lining, fastening direction and the position of a label. A wide shot establishes where that feature sits; a close detail view can then show its construction. Mark an unseen feature as unknown.
Compare the selling unit and size system

One listing might offer a single sweatshirt while the other offers a sweatshirt and matching trousers. Read the option description, quantity and subtotal after making the intended selection on both pages. Then compare size charts using the same measurement paths. A medium in one seller's pattern can differ from a medium on another page even when the photograph displays the same model.
Keep warehouse pictures with their source

A warehouse image found for seller A is evidence about the photographed unit from that listing. Do not move it into seller B's folder simply because the studio photographs match. If a gallery does not identify its source or option, keep its status clear. It might help you recognize a design detail to investigate, but does not resolve whether the seller you are considering currently supplies that detail.
Decide what further evidence would change your choice

Identify the one difference that matters. If you need a lined garment, a picture of the inside of the chosen version may settle the question. If you care about sleeve length, ask for the measurement and defined endpoints. Keep the two offers separate until the evidence answers that decision. A lower displayed price has little meaning until both columns describe the same contents, options and units.
Classify what kind of image you are comparing

A studio image usually tries to communicate an overall look. It may include a model, decorative props, coordinated garments or multiple colourways. A diagram can communicate dimensions or show a feature from a useful angle. A warehouse picture can show a particular unit after it was received. When comparing listings with the same thumbnail, write the origin of each image beside your observation. A denim jacket photographed with a matching belt does not establish that the belt ships with every version of the jacket.

A recognisable background can help you see that two images share the same underlying photograph. The same crease on a sleeve or identical reflection on a buckle gives you a clue. The clue relates to the image, not automatically to the identity of a supplier or the construction of the goods. Two shops may make different claims beside the same photograph. Compare those claims on their own terms and give more weight to evidence attached to the exact option being considered.
Pick details that change your buying decision

Suppose you need a work bag that fits a document folder without folding it. A side-by-side view of two matching front graphics will do little to answer your question. Look for internal opening width, usable depth, zipper shape and the position of any central divider. A listed exterior width might include thick sides or tapered corners. Ask for the particular dimension that controls whether the folder slides through the opening. Keep the folder dimensions beside your notes so the question has a defined purpose.

A different buyer may care primarily about strap attachment. For that buyer, an image of a metal ring stitched through a reinforced tab is more useful than a close view of the front graphic. Check both attachment points where possible and identify which listing supplied each view. The most helpful comparison depends on the intended use. A longer checklist of unrelated visual similarities can make two listings seem well researched while leaving the one purchasing requirement completely unanswered.
Read the specific seller commitments

Open both selected options and compare the words describing the contents. One seller may explicitly list a woven strap and an internal pouch, while the second shows both in a product photograph without specifying inclusion. Record the second listing's package contents as unclear. Contact that seller if the difference determines your choice. A positive answer from the first shop cannot resolve the second shop's offer, even if the same photograph and nearly identical product name appear on both pages.

Read measurements with similar care. A chart headed “approximate outer size” describes a different measurement from “usable opening.” If a screenshot cuts off the chart heading or its unit, obtain the full chart before comparing numbers. The better documented listing might offer fewer illustrations and still answer more of your actual questions. Conversely, a detailed specification can identify a potential fit problem even when every photograph looks visually identical to a product you previously purchased from another source.
Distinguish a seller change from a product difference

If both links lead to the same marketplace and item identifier, compare the selected options and the dates the pages were captured. A difference in price may arise because one capture shows an accessory, a different quantity, or an earlier version of the offer. If the identifiers differ, keep separate records even when the shop name matches. A seller may create multiple offers with different package quantities or terms while reusing studio assets. Those are different buying choices until the specific details reconcile.

A duplicate spreadsheet entry is a further possibility. If both grid cards link through to the same source listing with the same selected option, one set of current seller checks may serve both discoveries. Preserve their discovery links if you want to revisit the categories where you found them. Where the original listing is inaccessible, describe the relationship as unresolved. Guessing from two visually similar cards risks merging unrelated references and makes later order questions harder to reconstruct.
Write a conclusion that another buyer could check

An actionable comparison might read as follows. Both listings show the same green bag on a wooden stool. Seller A gives an opening width and includes an adjustable strap in the chosen option. Seller B gives exterior dimensions and does not describe the strap. The folder fit and strap inclusion are therefore unresolved for seller B. This note identifies the shared visual, the facts attributable to each seller and the remaining questions without rating either seller or making claims about stock quality.

If you purchase one version, add an observation about your own received unit beneath that seller's record. A photograph of the bag open with the stated contents visible can answer questions about the unit you received. It does not retrospectively verify another listing. Over time, this practice produces a small collection of comparable evidence with dates and option labels. When someone asks whether a visually similar find is the same product, you can point to the precise features established and the comparisons still missing.

articles.title: How to read a clothing label in KakoBuy warehouse photos
articles.lead: A label can answer the question printed on it. Separate marked size, garment measurements and care information so a single tiny picture does not have to carry three different conclusions.
sections: Identify which label you need

For a marked size, request the neckline, waistband or other label showing the garment's size. For care instructions or a stated fibre composition, ask for the relevant sewn-in information label, including the reverse if text continues there. A paper hangtag may contain the shop's stock number but can become detached. A label photographed alone is harder to associate with a specific piece than a view that also shows its position on the garment.
Ask for readable evidence

Describe what must be legible. A photograph taken square to the label under even lighting can reveal more than a high-resolution picture taken at a steep angle. Ask that folds are opened without tearing stitching. If the print is tiny, request a contextual photograph and one close view. Make sure both belong to the same warehouse entry, especially when your order includes two nearly identical colours.
Read size systems carefully

Some labels show multiple size systems or a combination of a letter and numbers. Copy the full line before translating it. Compare the seller's selected option and size chart with that line. A reference photo marked XL from an earlier order tells you what was printed on that photographed unit only. It does not establish the fit of the medium currently assigned to your order.
Check fit independently

Use a garment you already own as a physical comparison. For a shirt laid flat, you might measure underarm to underarm and back length from a named seam. Record the units and the way the garment was laid out. If the warehouse measurement uses a different endpoint or stretches a knit, repeat the measurement consistently before judging a discrepancy. Do not expect matching letters on two labels to eliminate pattern differences.
Present a clear mismatch

If you ordered a particular size and a photograph seems to show a different one, send the selected option and the image together. Explain exactly which marking is unexpected and ask the agent to check the actual unit. A label image cannot establish authenticity, the truth of a composition claim or the durability of a seam by itself. Report the observable difference and retain the response with the item record.
Identify the label that answers your question

A garment can carry several labels. A neck label can show a brand or a letter size. A sewn-in side label may carry composition and care information. A removable hangtag may show a merchant's stock code, price or barcode. Start by identifying the question and where its answer might actually appear. If your concern is whether a jacket is the ordered size, a clear photograph of a promotional hangtag may be less useful than a readable view of the size marking sewn into the received garment.

Labels can refer to different parts of one garment. A coat may have an outer shell, lining and padding identified on separate lines. If a photograph shows one percentage but crops out the part name, resist applying that figure to the entire coat. Request a view that includes both the part description and its composition line. Keep the seller's written specification beside the photo so a difference can be described precisely, for example a discrepancy affecting the lining rather than a general claim about the coat.
Preserve characters that are easy to misread

The difference between a small and a medium can be a single letter. The difference between two style numbers can be a leading zero, a dash or the final digit. Zoom in on the original file when possible. Upscaling an already blurred screenshot may make text look smoother without revealing the missing character. Transcribe only what you can actually read and mark an unclear position with a question mark. Someone checking later can then focus on that position in a replacement photograph.

A folded label can bring two unrelated lines next to each other. For a useful second view, ask to see the label unfolded on a flat surface with the complete text visible, subject to what the warehouse can provide. If the garment has several language blocks, look for a complete block rather than assembling percentages from fragments of different ones. Save the original image alongside any personal translation or cropped reference. This keeps the source available if a later reader questions a character or interpretation.
Use a size label together with a measurement

Suppose your order says medium and the sewn-in label also reads medium. That resolves the label comparison. It does not yet answer whether the garment will fit over your usual sweater. Compare the seller's size chart with the measurement you need, observing whether the chart describes garment width laid flat or a body circumference. For a jacket, a tape photograph running straight between underarm points can answer a practical fit question that a perfectly legible size label leaves open.

If the label says large while the order says medium, save both before deciding how to proceed. A seller may offer a written explanation or an order confirmation may show a different selected option from the one you recall. Record the explanation separately from your initial observation. Avoid overwriting the original selection in your notes simply because someone describes the items as fitting similarly. You may decide a measured garment works for you, but that is a separate decision from whether the label matches the order.
Consider what a label can actually prove

A photo can establish what is printed or sewn onto the photographed item when the connection between image and garment is clear. It cannot independently verify a fibre blend, an origin claim or authenticity. For a purchase that depends on a particular material, record both the seller's written description and the wording on the garment. Where the two conflict, ask for clarification before treating either as a confirmed material test. A missing label also leaves the relevant claim unverified in the available photos.

The context is particularly important with multipacks. One photo of a label on a black T-shirt cannot confirm the labels on two white T-shirts packed alongside it. Decide whether the same evidence is needed for each item. If the order contains mixed sizes, separate each garment by colour and ordered size in the request. A group overview plus a close view linked to each relevant garment can prevent a clear but isolated label image from being assigned to the wrong piece.
Build a clean note for the next decision

A useful clothing-label note can be just a few sentences. Identify the garment and selected option, state the visible wording, identify the unresolved question and specify whether it affects your decision. For example, the paid order says navy jacket, size medium. The label appears to read medium. A number at the bottom is cut off, but you only needed to confirm size. In that case the missing number need not generate another photo request or delay your decision.

When the missing text does matter, keep the request narrow. Ask for the full composition label on the navy jacket, including the shell and lining headings, with the tag unfolded enough to read both sections. Check any available service terms or price before requesting a paid detail view. After the new image arrives, add it beside the original rather than deleting the first image. The pair documents what prompted your question and which detail eventually resolved it.

articles.title: KakoBuy shoe QC: checking both shoes in the pair
articles.lead: A picture of one well-presented shoe cannot establish what is in the other half of the box. A paired inspection starts with identity and finishes with the specific features that affect your decision.
sections: Start with the pair you ordered

Write down the seller's size system, colour option and quantity. Keep that information with the warehouse entry. The carton label can be a useful cross-check, but it describes the carton. Ask to see the actual left and right shoes together in a frame. If several pairs arrived in one order, do not infer that every image in a gallery belongs to the first row of the purchase summary.
Use a paired view for symmetry

For a useful top view, ask for the shoes side by side on the same level surface, heels aligned and toes facing the same direction. Comparing a near shoe with a far shoe in an angled picture can exaggerate apparent size differences. A full back view gives a different comparison of heel height, seam position and colour. Decide which arrangement best displays the suspected issue before requesting more photographs.
Check each label independently

A single readable size label establishes a marking on one shoe. Ask for each label if size mismatch is the concern, and note the sizing system rather than comparing bare numbers. A US marking and a UK marking on the same label can be different without showing a mismatch. Compare the equivalent line on the left and right shoes against the option recorded in the order.
Define a length question precisely

If internal length matters and the insole is removable, ask whether removal is appropriate before requesting a measurement. A tape laid along the outside sole measures another object. Specify the endpoints, units and which shoe is measured. An insole length provides a physical dimension, but not an assurance of comfort: usable space also depends on shape, thickness and your own foot.
Distinguish design from damage

Some shoes deliberately have asymmetrical panels or different markings on left and right. Compare the official seller option pictures for the specific design rather than assuming every colour patch should mirror its partner. If the concern is a split seam or a scuff, request a focused close-up plus a wider picture identifying its location. Save both beside the purchase record and check the applicable next steps before dispatch.
Establish which shoe is which

Two pictures in a gallery do not necessarily show a pair. One could be the same shoe turned around. Begin with a view of both shoes together, with their toes pointing in the same direction. The inside and outside edges should then be easier to distinguish. If one shoe is partly inside the other or the heels are hidden behind packing paper, write down the missing view. A photograph of one excellent lateral profile gives little information about the second shoe.

If the order contains two identical-looking pairs in different sizes, keep their warehouse records separate. A shoe box label can provide context if it is clearly tied to the pair in the picture, but boxes and shoes are distinct objects. For a size-sensitive order, ask for the visible size marking inside each shoe and connect the photographs to the correct pair. A combined image showing the two heel openings can help, provided both labels remain legible when viewed at their original resolution.
Choose matched views for comparison

A photograph taken very close to one toe can make it look larger than the other. When comparing toe or heel shape, a matched overhead view with the pair side by side is more informative than two unrelated close-ups. Check whether the shoes sit equally far from the camera and both rest on the same flat surface. Differences in stuffing, lacing and angle can change the outline. Describe the feature you observe before guessing at a manufacturing or handling cause.

Use an overhead view for alignment, a rear view for heel height and a view of both outsoles for tread pattern. The same camera angle rarely answers all three questions. If the first images already show the tread and shape clearly, a request for another front view adds little. Request the single angle that could change your decision. For an apparent mismatch in heel colour, a view under the same light can be more helpful than a close-up taken in a different room.
Read size markings without inventing conversions

A shoe label may list several regional size systems on separate lines. Transcribe the whole relevant line with its unit or system. A numerical marking from one system and another marking from a different system can look unequal while describing the same paired product. Compare like with like across both shoes and against the seller's selected option. If a label is hidden by the tongue, ask for a view of the label face rather than guessing from the visible end of the number.

For practical fit, compare a reference pair you own using the same measurement method the seller describes. A removable insole length and an outsole length are different measurements. A buyer who knows the insole of a comfortable shoe should ask for an equivalent measurement only if the item and service permit it. A photo where a ruler begins outside the heel or follows a visibly curved path can give a misleading comparison. Specify where the measurement should start and finish when the difference matters.
Distinguish presentation from a physical difference

Packing paper can create an apparent bulge and a loose lace can make one opening look larger. For something you suspect to be a physical mismatch, note whether the feature persists across another angle. A shadow at the sidewall in a front view may disappear in a side image. A clearly different tread pattern visible across the whole outsole is a different kind of observation. State the visible feature and ask the person handling the order to check it directly if necessary.

Consider an example where one shoe has a dark mark near the heel. Record which shoe and whether the mark appears on the material or only on nearby wrapping. A second image with the wrapping moved away could resolve that ambiguity. It may not identify what the mark is or whether it can be removed. Avoid promising that brushing or washing will solve it. If surface condition affects your purchase, obtain a sufficiently clear view and ask what options are available for this order.
Keep pair condition and box condition separate

A crushed box lid can matter for gifting or storage even if the shoes appear intact. Torn wrapping can be visible without revealing whether either shoe is damaged. Record package condition and item condition separately. If the box is essential, check whether the exact option included the box and whether requested packing services address it before international dispatch. A retailer-style studio photo of a branded box is weaker evidence of inclusion than a written option description or the warehouse's record of what arrived.

When all required views are available, close the inspection with a short statement about both shoes. For example, both labels display the ordered system and size, both outsoles show the same tread and the left heel has a visible mark that still needs clarification. This record is more useful than a single “QC passed” line because it explains the specific checks you completed. Keep the images with the order in case a later packing or exchange question refers to one shoe in particular.

articles.title: A missing strap, cable or pouch: documenting a KakoBuy accessory issue
articles.lead: An accessory can be missing from a photograph, omitted from a selected option, packed out of view or genuinely absent from the received order. Resolve those possibilities in sequence.
sections: Establish what the option included

Find the order confirmation and the selected seller description. Highlight the wording that identifies the accessory, quantity and version. A shoulder bag worn with a decorative strap in a studio photograph might have separate options with and without that strap. A product title saying kit could describe more than one package. Start the inquiry with what the seller offered for the option you purchased.
Inspect what the available photo actually shows

A closed box or zipped bag is an incomplete view of its contents. Note whether the packaging is open, which compartments are visible and whether an accessory could be wrapped separately. A small cable can sit under a cardboard insert; detachable clips can be inside an inner pocket. Avoid asking the warehouse to break seals or dismantle an item before you understand whether this affects its condition or return eligibility.
Request an inventory view

Name the missing piece and describe where it may be packed. Ask for an overview with the unit and all loose contents together, followed by a detail view if the shape or connector matters. Give the warehouse entry number so the inspection concerns the unit you actually bought. If another box from the same seller is still in transit, ask whether the accessory is supposed to travel separately.
Write down an evidence-based conclusion

Suppose your order names a pouch and two clips. The overview shows one pouch, one loose clip and a second clip attached to the bag. That photograph supports a complete count even though only one clip appears loose. In another case a photograph might show unopened packaging and no clips, leaving the count unresolved. Describe what can be counted and what remains hidden.
Keep the resolution tied to the original purchase

If the seller offers to send a missing piece, record its promised description and new domestic tracking number. If an exchange is offered, retain the original item reference and the replacement reference separately. Do not mark the case complete simply because a message promises a shipment. Close the record when the received accessory can be identified and checked against the original option.
Establish whether the accessory was included

A practical accessory check starts with the wording attached to your paid selection. Suppose a bag appears in a studio photograph beside a leather strap, a decorative charm and a dust cover. The actual option might describe only the bag and shoulder strap. Save the option text and any written seller confirmation you relied on. Treat the charm and dust cover separately unless you have evidence that the seller included them in that particular offer. This makes an inquiry clearer and avoids claiming that every photographed prop was purchased.

Read the units carefully. A listing might offer a set of replacement clips, a strap sold without clips or a bundle containing both. The order quantity tells you how many units of the chosen offer you purchased. It does not by itself define the number of components inside each unit. Make a short expected-contents list in plain language. For example, one bag, one detachable shoulder strap and two clips already attached to the ends of that strap. Such a description gives the warehouse specific objects to look for.
Separate an unseen item from a confirmed shortage

In a first warehouse overview, a strap might be inside the bag, under tissue paper or attached behind the handle. A single photograph of the closed bag cannot establish a shortage. Ask whether the contents can be checked and, if permitted, request a view that shows the open bag and the loose components beside it. Avoid requesting removal of sealed packaging until you understand the implications for that order and have decided that opening it is appropriate.

If an accessory is visible but its identity is unclear, describe it by location and appearance. A narrow black strip seen behind a bag could be a handle, a shoulder strap or a piece of packaging. A photograph of its attachment clips or its full length might distinguish those possibilities. Where access or image quality still prevents confirmation, leave the status as unresolved. The accuracy of the record matters more than reaching a confident conclusion from an ambiguous view.
Handle accessories packed separately

A seller might send more than one parcel for a purchase. Before assuming a component has been omitted, check the records the order shows for expected domestic deliveries and warehouse intake. Distinguish a seller message saying an item will follow from a shipment reference or intake entry that actually identifies it. If a second package exists, record the reference and what it is expected to contain. Keep the purchase open for the outstanding component until you can evaluate the evidence relevant to your decision.

A second domestic tracking event also does not prove the missing accessory is inside. The event identifies movement of a package. The received contents require a corresponding intake record or confirmation. For a bag with a detachable chain strap, you might note that the main bag arrived on one date and the seller described a separate parcel for the chain on another date. Link the second intake to the purchase only once the order record or support response gives you a basis to do so.
Ask for a specific next action

A useful message includes the selected option, the privately supplied order reference, the component expected and the evidence currently available. You might write that the paid selection says bag with long strap, the overview shows the bag closed and the strap is not visible. Ask whether someone can check inside the bag and confirm the strap before dispatch. This describes a gap and requests a specific action without accusing the seller or warehouse of losing an item.

If support confirms the item was absent, ask which resolution options apply to this order and whether each one involves a deadline, charge or separate shipment. A replacement accessory, a seller inquiry and a return can have different consequences. Record what you actually request and any confirmation received. Avoid combining the missing-strap question with unrelated complaints about colour or packaging in one long paragraph. Separate observations make it easier to see which issues have been addressed and which remain open.
Close the record with evidence of the outcome

A promise to send an accessory resolves the seller's intended next step. The actual shortage remains open until the promised item arrives or you accept another resolution. Keep the follow-up intake, photograph or adjustment alongside the original order. If an adjustment is offered, record the amount, currency and scope in the private order notes. A statement about one accessory does not automatically explain other charges or establish a general policy for future orders.

At the packing stage, check that the final parcel request still includes every warehouse item needed for the complete set. If a replacement strap has a separate warehouse reference, attach or select it as the current interface requires. If support says it was already placed inside the bag, save that confirmation. A precise final note can be very short: the black long strap arrived separately, the clips are visible in the new image, and the bag and strap now belong to the same intended parcel.

articles.title: Writing a useful KakoBuy detail-photo request before shipping
articles.lead: A useful request tells a person holding the item what to photograph, how to position it and which question the resulting frame should answer.
sections: Write the decision first

Explain what changes depending on the result. You might need to decide whether a jacket has a two-way zipper, whether a printed name is spelled correctly, or whether a sleeve is long enough. The phrase more pictures leaves the photographer to choose an angle. Starting with the decision helps you ask for one informative view rather than several attractive views that repeat the original gallery.
Identify the object unambiguously

Give the item or order reference and exact option. When two navy jackets differ only in size, a colour name is insufficient. Ask that the item remains identifiable in the picture. For a personalisation check, provide the exact text from the order and specify whether front, back or sleeve should be visible. Avoid including unrelated personal or payment information in the request.
Specify composition and endpoints

For a zipper, ask for a closed full-front view with both ends and any sliders visible. For a flat garment width, describe the seam points and ask that the tape's beginning and reading appear in one frame. For a print, ask for a straight-on view that shows placement and another view only if the text is too small. A tightly cropped image may improve legibility while removing the context needed to identify the unit.
Check the response against the question

Look at the requested feature before scanning the rest of the photograph. Can you see both endpoints? Is the label readable? Is the unit laid flat, or held at an angle that distorts the apparent length? If the image leaves a gap, describe that gap in a follow-up. Asking for the lower slider to be visible is more actionable than saying that the first picture was bad.
Budget the service and retain the result

Check availability, fees and processing information in the current KakoBuy order flow. A third-party article can suggest useful angles, but the conditions attached to your own order decide which request can be fulfilled. Once the image arrives, keep it with the original request and the decision you made. A dated note explaining the accepted measurement remains useful if the item later becomes part of a multi-item parcel.
Write the question before selecting the view

Begin by finishing a sentence such as “I need this photo to decide whether the folder will fit inside the sleeve.” A question with a concrete decision helps you choose the subject, angle and reference point. If the sleeve opens along one edge, the useful view might show the clear opening between the two zipper stops. A photo of the entire bag laid beside a ruler can look informative while leaving that exact opening hidden by the zipper or by folded fabric.

An item can invite many interesting close-ups. Prioritise the one detail that determines whether you will accept it. For a garment bought for layering, the flat chest width may be more important than a logo close-up. For a bag bought to replace a lost part, the attachment clip and its inner width may matter most. Use the available gallery to eliminate questions already answered. A focused request takes less interpretation and makes it easier to recognise whether the resulting photo actually satisfies your purpose.
Describe a location anyone can find

Use an object and a landmark instead of ambiguous directions. “The inside seam below the left arm when the jacket is worn” identifies a different spot from “the seam on the left of my screen.” Where possible, attach a cropped reference with the area circled and retain a wider view that establishes its location. A close crop of two black seams can be hard to locate on a dark garment. The wide view gives the photographer a way to identify the correct area.

For a pair or a set, name the component as well. A request for the tongue label can produce a clear image of the right shoe while your question concerns the left. If both need checking, say so explicitly and explain what must be readable. A request for a bag buckle should specify which strap and whether the buckle should be shown open, closed or from the inside. Each detail serves an actual comparison and helps avoid a repetition of the existing overview.
Specify how a measurement should be taken

For a flat garment measurement, state the start point, end point and unit. If you want the width across a sweatshirt under the arms, ask to see the garment laid flat, the tape beginning at one underarm seam and ending at the other, with both ends visible. Avoid asking for a fit verdict from a picture. Compare the resulting measurement with a garment you own taken by the same method, and keep any material stretch or garment shape in mind.

For a small opening, a wide view with both ends of a ruler readable may be more useful than a very tight close-up. A cropped photograph of the number at the far end does not establish the starting point. If a rigid object needs to pass through the opening, distinguish the usable gap from the overall length of the closing hardware. In your note, state which measurement you received. Keep an approximate reading separate from any conclusion about whether the object will fit comfortably.
Adapt the request to realistic handling

Some details can be shown by rotating an item. Others require opening packaging, removing a tag or disassembling a component. Identify what the photo would require and check whether the service can perform that action. If it would affect a seal or condition important to your purchase, stop and decide whether the evidence is worth that change. A request to show a manufacturer's printed seal from the outside may answer part of the question with less handling.

If the available service offers a priced photo option, check the displayed scope before using it. Confirm whether you are ordering a single image, a requested angle or another defined service. Avoid assuming that adding five unrelated instructions to one message guarantees five separate results. If you have a fixed budget for inspection, choose the detail with the greatest impact on your decision and specify what would count as a readable answer. Save the confirmation with your order evidence.
Evaluate the result and decide whether to follow up

Open the original result rather than judging it from a thumbnail. Check three things: whether it is the correct item, whether it shows the specified area and whether the detail is readable or measurable. If it answers your question, write down the observation and date. A concise note such as “zip opening is visible between both stops, measured across the usable gap” preserves the basis of your decision more clearly than a generic acceptance mark.

If the result misses one requirement, quote that requirement and identify what the image did show. For example, the photograph shows the zipper's total length, while the usable opening between the stops remains hidden. Ask for that specific change only if it still matters to the order. If photography cannot settle the issue, consider the seller's written answer, the available order options or declining the purchase. Repeating the same unanswerable request is unlikely to produce stronger evidence.

articles.title: Tracking a KakoBuy exchange from the original purchase to the replacement
articles.lead: An exchange creates a second physical unit. Keep the original promise, the original problem and the replacement evidence connected without mixing their identifiers.
sections: Preserve the starting point

Save the seller option, quantity, price and original order reference. Keep the warehouse photographs that identify the problem. State the issue in terms another person could verify, such as the received size tag reading large when the paid selection was medium. A general statement that the item looks different is harder to act on when the seller page has multiple versions or a changing set of pictures.
Check the available remedy

Read the instructions on the actual order and ask what the seller or platform needs before the unit is moved. Note any requirement concerning packaging, tags, evidence or domestic return transport. Avoid assuming that storage time and exchange eligibility have the same deadline. A return agreement, a dispatched return and an accepted replacement are distinct events and may have separate references.
Record the original unit's movement

Retain the original warehouse entry even after the unit has left. Add the domestic tracking number if one is provided and record who supplied it. A carrier scan tells you about the physical delivery of a package. It cannot, on its own, show that a seller inspected the item, accepted the exchange or sent the replacement. Update each step only when its own evidence appears.
Check the replacement without recycling the old pictures

Give the replacement a separate line with its warehouse intake reference and photographs. Verify the precise detail that prompted the exchange and check the rest of the unit as well. A corrected colour does not establish the right size, quantity or included accessories. When the photographs look identical to the original set, ask which images belong to the new intake before treating them as fresh evidence.
Close both the item and payment records

Record any additional charge or credit using the amount, currency and payee actually shown. Match the amounts to the relevant order rather than quietly changing the old price. The item record can be resolved once the replacement has been checked and accepted, even if a separate credit remains pending. Keep both statuses visible to avoid submitting the wrong unit for international packing.
Define the replacement you would accept

Before requesting an exchange, write down the exact option that would resolve your problem. If a seller delivered a blue shirt in medium when you ordered navy in medium, the remedy may be the originally selected navy option. If you ordered medium and now decide you want large, describe that as a change of selection. The difference matters because the seller and agent need to understand what happened and what item you would accept. Preserve the original order wording in both situations.

Think through alternatives before someone offers a substitute. You might accept a larger size only if a measured chest width falls within a particular range. You might accept the same colour in a different fabric only after seeing the new specification and price. Keep these conditions private until relevant, then state them explicitly when agreeing to a change. A message saying another option is available is a proposal. Record your answer and make sure the order record or later confirmation describes the choice you actually approved.
Build the timeline from events

Imagine the original garment arrived on Monday. On Tuesday you requested a different size. On Wednesday the agent asked the seller whether that size was in stock. At that point, the exchange has been requested and the seller response is outstanding. An estimate of when a replacement might arrive is not evidence that the original has been sent back or another garment dispatched. Keep the latest confirmed event and the next expected event on separate lines so you can follow up with a precise question.

Useful event fields are date, actor, item or parcel reference, action and evidence. A support reply, tracking event, payment adjustment or new warehouse photograph may each support a different line. Where a time is important, retain the time zone shown in the original record. Do not count an estimate as an elapsed deadline unless the relevant order terms or a support message establish one. If a return or exchange option is time-sensitive, ask support which deadline applies to the specific order.
Keep outgoing and incoming tracking apart

An exchange may involve an outgoing domestic parcel and an incoming replacement. They have different directions and can have different tracking references. Label each reference by direction. If an outgoing parcel shows delivered, that event can help establish that a parcel reached its domestic destination. It does not confirm that the seller inspected it, approved a replacement, dispatched the replacement or that the warehouse received the correct size. Ask about the first missing step instead of repeating the entire timeline.

If a replacement is associated with a new order or warehouse number, connect it to the original using a dated note. Avoid changing the original number to the new one and losing the connection. The original record documents the paid selection and the first unit. The replacement record documents what arrived later. If the replacement is bundled with another item, make sure your note identifies which piece belongs to the exchange and which piece belongs to an unrelated purchase.
Follow the money separately

A price difference, domestic delivery charge or service charge may be discussed during an exchange. Ask which amounts apply to the offered resolution, which currency they use and whether you need to approve them before work proceeds. A quoted amount is not a payment. Record a charge only when you see the corresponding transaction or confirmation. Likewise, a promised refund and a completed credit may appear on different dates. Tracking the money separately prevents unexplained changes to the item's original purchase price.

Suppose a seller proposes a more expensive size variant and separately mentions delivery back to the warehouse. Record the item difference and delivery amount as separate fields, even if they later appear as one payment. Check what that payment covers before agreeing. If the transaction appears in another currency, preserve the original amount as well as the amount actually charged. The numbers remain attributable even if your card statement later includes a conversion or a fee outside the seller's quote.
Inspect the replacement as a new unit

When a new garment arrives, repeat the checks that triggered the exchange. A warehouse status confirming receipt does not tell you whether the new size label or measurement meets your requirement. Compare the replacement against the written agreement and the photos attached to its own intake. If the original problem involved a crooked fastening, inspect that detail on the replacement instead of relying on the original unit's photos. Also confirm the basic option and quantity so a different mistake does not slip through.

Once you have decided, record the result, remaining charges or credits and the warehouse reference intended for international dispatch. Check that the parcel selection uses the accepted replacement. If an old record still appears in your account, do not assume it represents an additional dispatchable item. Ask support which reference corresponds to the unit now held if anything is unclear. A completed timeline ends with a specific accepted item or another confirmed resolution and makes later parcel questions much easier to answer.

articles.title: When a seller changes a KakoBuy listing after you save or buy it
articles.lead: A stable marketplace link can lead to a page whose option wording, photographs or price has changed. Compare dated records before deciding what the change means for your order.
sections: Capture a useful snapshot

Save the seller page with the chosen option visible, the original option text, price, quantity and item ID. Include a date. For a set, make sure the included pieces are stated somewhere in the record. A screenshot of the hero image alone contains little information about which bundle was selected. Keep the agent purchase confirmation separately because it records the choice submitted through the order.
Identify the layer that changed

A change in translated wording may occur even when the original seller option is unchanged. Compare original text, option code if available, thumbnail, selected unit and live price. If the whole listing now opens at a different default, select the old option manually before drawing a conclusion. A changed default and a discontinued version call for different decisions.
Reprice an unpaid shortlist entry

If you have not paid, treat a changed quantity or bundle as a new comparison. Recalculate the unit cost for the included contents, check current stock and review the size chart for the new option. Do not force the old cost into your new shortlist because the listing number is unchanged. If the changed term was the feature you wanted, leave the entry unresolved until the seller confirms it.
Compare a paid order to the agreement at payment

Keep the new listing as evidence of its present state, but compare the received unit with your order-time selection. If your original record said jacket and detachable hood and the current page says jacket only, quote both versions with their dates when asking for a check. The fact that today’s page omits the hood does not independently prove what was selected earlier.
Reassess historical QC references

An album tied to the same marketplace identifier may show a version sold before the edit. Check the recording date, label, visible construction and package contents. Use it as a guide to the detail worth checking rather than evidence of the new offer. If your own current warehouse pictures become available, connect them to their order and option first and document any specific difference before deciding about shipping.
Save the offer as a dated selection

A product link can continue working while its option names, photographs, price or package contents change. If a particular detail determines your choice, save that detail at the time you decide. For a travel pouch, keep the selected option wording, its dimensions, the included strap description and the quantity you are buying. A dated screenshot with the selected option and its price visible can support the note. Crop out private account information when sharing it outside the order support channel.

A seller's headline may continue to say “travel pouch with strap” when a newly added option sells the strap alone. Review the selected option and resulting subtotal instead of relying on the headline. If possible, capture both the seller's wording and your working translation. Revisit the selection just before submitting an order, particularly if it has remained in a cart for several days. A previous research note explains why you shortlisted the item; the current selection controls what you are about to submit.
Distinguish a renamed option from a different offer

Suppose an option once called “olive large” now appears as “green B.” The names alone do not establish whether the products match. Compare the seller's current dimensions, materials, quantity and included components with the original record. If the seller displays an internal option code, compare it as additional evidence, keeping the marketplace item identifier separate. A continuing item identifier establishes the listing reference. The seller may still have changed one or more choices inside that listing.

Look for the size chart heading and product diagram associated with the active option. A listing can share one gallery across multiple options, so scrolling past a familiar diagram does not always attach that diagram to your selected version. If the difference matters, ask the seller a question that identifies both old and new wording. A question about whether “green B” currently contains the large pouch and detachable strap gives a clearer target than asking whether the whole page is still the same.
Handle a change before you pay

If you have only shortlisted the product, you can reassess its current terms without reconstructing an order dispute. Record the new option as a fresh observation, compare it with your original requirement and decide whether to keep it on your list. If the new selling unit is one pouch instead of a set of two, recalculate the quantity and subtotal before comparing it with another seller. A superficially unchanged item price can represent a different value when the number of pieces changes.

If a selector remains ambiguous, leave the purchase pending while you investigate. A product note saying “send the old version” does not give the seller the old stock or guarantee that an agent can select it. Ask whether the precise old version is available and how to identify it in the current order flow. Preserve any answer with the date. If the response points to a different listing, treat it as a new source and check the actual option text on that listing.
Handle a change after payment

For an existing order, begin with the paid selection and confirmation, then compare the revised public offer. A listing edit alone does not establish what was ordered or what the seller shipped. If support asks whether you will accept a substitute, ask for its option wording, important differences and any price adjustment before answering. Keep your response paired with that proposal. A simple “yes” copied out of context may be difficult to interpret if multiple alternatives were discussed.

A practical support message can say that your paid order shows a large olive pouch with a detachable strap, while the current page describes green B without specifying a strap. Ask which version was purchased for your order and whether the strap is included. Provide the dated order reference privately and attach the relevant excerpts. If the answer depends on checking the incoming unit, record that as the next step and decide which warehouse photograph or contents check would settle the issue.
Update shared finds without erasing the history

If you share findings with others, keep the original dated note and add an update. Explain the particular change you observed and what you have yet to confirm. For example, the old label disappeared and the listing now offers green A and green B, while the correspondence with the former size remains unknown. A reader can then decide whether your older warehouse album is useful for the shape of the pouch or too uncertain for their current option decision.

After a received unit is photographed, connect its observations to the paid selection and any approved substitution. Do not promote one order's outcome into a promise that every purchase from the edited listing will receive the same version. If the new option works for your own purpose, state the feature that made it acceptable and retain the related evidence. A future buyer may value a different detail and will be able to judge whether your dated comparison answers their question.
